catalog_quote: In many languages, especially Indo-European languages, stress is a reliable marker of phonological words. This is because the placement of stress in such languages is predictable, always falling on a syllable in a particular position. As is the case in many tone languages of West Africa, stress does not play a significant role at the word level and is therefore unhelpful in determining phonological words. For instance, Dakubu (1981:235) finds that in Gã, as in Yoruba, the domain of semantically based syllable stress is not the word but the pause group (i.e. the intonation unit). [p. 41] ... Tone plays a very important role in Gã. The language has both lexical and grammatical tone. It has two phonemic tones: High (H) and Low (L). ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Ga is a two-tone (H/L, with downstepped H; terrace-level) language. Word-level stress plays no significant role and does not mark the phonological word; what stress there is ('semantically based syllable stress', i.e. emphasis/prominence) is a property of the pause group / intonation unit, not of the word (Campbell citing Dakubu 1981:235). No word-stress position is given because none is claimed.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Campbell. Older contrary-looking statement: Zimmermann 1858 §4 (pp. 5-6) says word 'accentuation' is 'generally on the root of the word and in compound words.. on the fundamental component', and the possessive pronoun takes the accent over its noun; but Zimmermann himself says the accent/intonation systems were 'not yet sufficiently ascertained', and his 'accent' predates tonal analysis.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain explicitly the pause group / intonation unit (phrase level), not the word; statement is about running speech, not citation forms. Alternative reading label: phrase-level prominence only. The word-level claim ('stress does not play a significant role at the word level') is Campbell's own; the pause-group finding is attributed to Dakubu 1981, which was not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Campbell 2017 describes Gã as spoken in Accra (the standard/central variety; she notes dialects in 1.3.1 but the description is not dialect-specific); Zimmermann 1858 describes the same Accra ('Akra') Gã of the 1850s. Both = gaaa1244; no differently named variety involved.
